title: Rapid capacity injection and backfill — runbook (WIP)
content:
Purpose:
This is a working runbook for rapidly injecting capacity and performing backfill during infra failures that affect GPU-backed node pools, plus safe node cordon/drain and recovery sequences. Intended for on-call SREs and infra engineers. Focus is on minimal blast radius, fast verification, and clear escalation points.

When to use this runbook:
- Node pool unexpectedly loses > 15% of GPU capacity or loses capacity for > 5 minutes.
- Multiple P95 latency/P99 errors on inference routes tied to capacity alerts.
- Planned emergency capacity add during traffic spike where autoscaling cannot catch up.

Prereqs / what you need before you start:
- Access: GCP/AWS console, cluster kubeconfig with cluster-admin, Terraform/infra repo access, internal VPN, Slack + escalation phone numbers.
- Tooling: kubectl, gcloud and/or aws CLI, terraform, ssh access to bastion if on-prem, nvidia-smi on nodes via ssh.
- Test harness: short inference smoke script (scripts/smoke/inference_smoke.py) and load generator (locust/simple curl loop).
- Dashboard check: Grafana "infra/gpu-pools" and "inference/latency-by-route" are up in your dashboard list.

High-level flow (short):
1) Triage: confirm alert, scope impact, create incident ticket.
2) Contain: if failing node(s) present, cordon and drain safely.
3) Inject capacity: increase managed node pool / ASG or provision hot spare nodes.
4) Backfill: schedule/force pods onto new nodes, watch scheduler and PDBs.
5) Verify: smoke tests, Grafana, canary routing.
6) Stabilize & post-ops: monitor, collect logs, hand to oncall return or owners, post-incident write-up.

Detailed steps:
A) Triage (first 10 minutes)
- Confirm the alert: open Grafana alert link, check Prometheus firing rule (example: GPUUtilizationHigh or NodeReadyMissing).
- Run quick health commands:
  - kubectl get nodes -o wide | egrep "gpu|accelerator"
  - kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o wide | egrep "CrashLoopBackOff|ImagePullBackOff|Pending"
  - kubectl get pdb --all-namespaces
  - kubectl top nodes | sort -k2 -nr  (confirm per-node CPU/GPU pressure if node-exporter exposes GPU metrics)
- Identify impacted node pool(s): label, taint, or node group name.
- Create an incident: create ticket SRE-<YYYYMMDD>-<INC> with summary and initial hypothesis. Post to #sre-incident with short summary, links, and who is owning.

B) Contain (safe cordon/drain)
- Before draining, check PodDisruptionBudgets (PDBs) and stateful workloads. If a PDB prevents disruption, pause and escalate to app-owner.
  - kubectl get pdb -A | grep <app-namespace>
- Cordon the node to stop new scheduling:
  - kubectl cordon <node-name>
- Drain the node (prefer graceful):
  - kubectl drain <node-name> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --pod-selector='!redwood-critical' --grace-period=300 --timeout=600s
  Notes: we use a pod-selector to avoid hitting system-critical pods; adjust --grace-period if apps need more time.
- If pods refuse to evict (stuck Pending due to local storage), escalate and consider --force with extreme caution. Document which pods were force-evicted.
- Validate drain: kubectl get pods --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node-name> -A | grep -v "DaemonSet"

C) Hardware/Driver swap (when node is physically faulty / on-prem)
- Confirm node fails nvidia-smi or GPU drivers: ssh to node and run sudo nvidia-smi.
- If GPU hardware replacement required, follow hardware vendor steps. Key checks before physical swap:
  - Record instance id, serial numbers, node kubelet logs (/var/log/kubelet.log), and dmesg output.
  - Create vendor RMA ticket with serial and failure timestamps. Use template: "RMA request: node=<instance-id>, GPU serial=<sn>, failure_time=<UTC time>, logs attached".
- If replacing local GPU card: schedule a short maintenance window and move remaining critical pods off the rack using drain sequence above.

D) Rapid capacity injection (cloud-managed node pools)
- If using GKE (example): increase node pool size or create a new node pool with same image and GPU type:
  - gcloud container node-pools resize <pool-name> --cluster=<cluster> --num-nodes=<desired> --region=<region>
  - Or create new pool: gcloud container node-pools create spare-gpu-pool --cluster=<cluster> --machine-type=n1-standard-16 --accelerator type=nvidia-tesla-t4,count=1 --image-type=UBUNTU
- If using AWS (EKS + ASG): update ASG desired capacity or spin up a launch-template-based group:
  - aws autoscaling set-desired-capacity --auto-scaling-group-name <asg-name> --desired-capacity <N> --honor-cooldown
  - Alternatively, create a temporary on-demand ASG for immediate capacity and add node-label bootstrap script.
- If using Terraform-managed infra, prefer using the infra repo and terraform apply to keep state consistent. Example workflow:
  - git checkout infra/compute && git pull && edit vars to increase pool size
  - terraform plan -var='gpu_pool_size=<new>' && terraform apply -var='gpu_pool_size=<new>'
  Note: If time-critical, perform cloud console change and follow up with a later TF drift fix. Document both steps in the incident ticket.

E) Backfill & scheduling hints
- After new nodes come up, ensure GPU drivers and container runtime are healthy. Quick checks on a new node:
  - ssh to node -> sudo nvidia-smi (should list GPU and driver version)
  - systemctl status docker/containerd
  - kubectl describe node <node> | egrep "Taints|Labels"
- Remove any temporary taints that prevent scheduling (e.g., node.kubernetes.io/unschedulable): kubectl uncordon <node>
- If pods are stuck pending, inspect scheduling errors: kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n <ns>
- If kube-scheduler prefers older pools, consider using rollout or eviction to speed placement:
  - Use Deployment strategy: kubectl rollout restart deploy/<deployment> -n <ns> for non-critical services to force re-schedule onto new nodes.
  - For stateful workloads with PVCs, prefer manual replica replacement respecting PDBs.

F) Canary verification and smoke tests
- Run smoke script against dedicated canary route and measure success rate (we use canary route /v1/infer?model=canary):
  - python3 scripts/smoke/inference_smoke.py --url https://canary.redwood.internal/v1/infer --count 100 --timeout 10
- Check latency and error budget on Grafana panels:
  - inference/latency-by-route p50/p95/p99 (target p95 <= 300ms for canary under nominal load)
  - infra/gpu-pools node-ready-count and gpu-utilization per node
- Confirm traffic fallback: ensure routing policies are sending X% traffic to hosted fallback model if configured.

G) Rollback / scale-down safe plan (after incident)
- Do not immediately tear down newly created nodes. Keep buffer for 1–6 hours depending on incident severity and traffic variance.
- If capacity injection was via console (not TF), make a follow-up TF change or create a cleanup PR to re-align state.
- When scaling down ASG/node pool, do it gradually and prefer cordon/drain sequence rather than instant termination.

H) Monitoring & logs to collect (during and post)
- kubelet logs: /var/log/kubelet.log on affected nodes.
- dmesg and syslog for hardware errors.
- NVIDIA logs: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=... and /var/log/nvidia-installer.log
- Prometheus queries to run quickly:
  - sum(node_gpu_total_gpus) by (node)
  - sum(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total) by (node)
  - increase(kube_node_status_condition{condition="Ready",status="false"}[5m])
- Save screenshots of Grafana panels and attach to ticket.

I) Communication & escalation
- Primary on-call: @sre-oncall in Slack. If primary cannot handle within 15 minutes escalate to SRE L2: @emma.t or phone +1-510-555-0183.
- If incident impacts enterprise customers or breaches SLA, notify support@redwood.com and the account owner immediately with the incident ticket link.
- Use incident channel #incident-<id> for all operational chatter; avoid spamming #sre.

J) Post-incident actions (owners and tickets)
- Owner: assign to eng-site-reliability engineer who ran the recovery.
- Required follow-ups within 72 hours:
  - Root-cause analysis and RCA doc with timeline.
  - If manual/console changes made, ensure Terraform state reconciled and PR created to make infra changes persistent.
  - Create capacity improvement task if autoscaler lag or wrong scaling metrics caused the incident.
  - Hardware RMA follow-up if physical GPU replaced.

Quick checklists (copyable)
- Incident creation checklist: create ticket, post to Slack, set status to "investigating", add links to dashboards.
- Node cordon/drain checklist: check PDBs -> cordon -> drain -> validate pods -> remove from LB if necessary -> mark node for hardware/repair.
- Capacity injection checklist: confirm image+driver -> scale node pool -> validate node readiness -> uncordon -> watch scheduler -> run smoke tests.

Common pitfalls and tips
- Do not force-evict stateful pods without talking to owners. PDBs exist for a reason.
- Beware of TF drift when making console changes in emergencies. Always follow up with commit/PR.
- Watch for daemonset GPU driver installation time. New nodes may appear Ready but GPU driver might be missing; nvidia-smi is the ground truth.
- For cost-sensitive bursts, prefer short-lived on-demand ASG pools labelled "ephemeral-emergency" to avoid long-term billing surprises.

Open questions / work-in-progress (this doc is WIP):
- Standardize an automated "warm spare" node pool in every region to avoid manual creation during incidents.
- Better integration of pod eviction prioritization with PDB-aware emergency scaling.
- Add templated vendor RMA request flow in the incident system.

Authors / contributors:
- Drafted by: Ravi Patel (SRE)
- Contributors: Emma Torres (SRE L2), Chen Li (Infra eng), Maya Gonzales (Platform ops)

Revision history:
- 2024-08-14: initial notes and checklist
- 2024-10-02: added cloud quick commands and TF guidance
- 2025-01-22: updated verification steps and escalation phone number

End of runbook (WIP). Please add edit notes inline and link final PRs/infra changes to the linked_artifacts list.
